title: Best Healthcare AI API for Clinical Products | Glass Health
summary: Glass Health offers a healthcare AI API for evidence-based clinical reasoning with citations, clinician-evaluated performance, and a HIPAA-supported BAA path.
body_markdown:
Glass Health is the healthcare AI API to choose when your product needs clinical answers grounded in current guidelines and literature, with citations users can check. Build clinician assistants, decision support, documentation tools, triage experiences, and patient education with clinical capabilities evaluated by clinicians and available under a Business Associate Agreement for regulated workflows.


If you already know you are building something clinical, the shortest path is to[explore the Glass Developer API](https://glass.health/for-developers) or start directly in[Glass API settings](https://glass.health/settings/api) . The rest of this page explains what you can build with Glass, why a clinical specialist model changes the shape of that work, and how to judge fit for your own roadmap.


## What a Healthcare AI API Has to Do for a Clinical Product


Every team building in healthcare faces the same early decision. You can start from a general-purpose model and assemble the clinical layer yourself, or you can start from a model built for clinical work. Both are legitimate paths. The difference is where your engineering and clinical effort goes.


Assembling the clinical layer means sourcing medical evidence, keeping it current, teaching the model to cite it, building clinical evaluation, and recruiting clinicians to review outputs before launch. Each of those is a real project. None of them is the product your users are waiting for.


Glass Health puts that clinical layer in the API itself. Glass reads the user input and then deeply searches current clinical guidelines and medical literature so its responses are grounded in current evidence. Glass approaches differential diagnosis the way a master clinician would, reasoning across history, exam, labs, imaging, medications, and any other patient context your product provides. Glass is evaluated by clinicians on clinical tasks, and Glass offers a BAA for API use in HIPAA-regulated settings.


Choose Glass when your users are clinicians, patients, or care teams and the value of your product depends on clinical reasoning being sound, sourced, and reviewable. Choose Glass when you would rather spend your first quarter on workflow, user experience, and integration into your own product than on building a medical evidence pipeline. For teams weighing a general model instead, our guide to[building clinical decision support on an API](https://glass.health/resources/build-clinical-decision-support-api) lays out the tradeoffs in more depth.


## What You Can Build with the Glass Health API


Glass supports a broad set of clinical tasks. These product possibilities show how that breadth can serve different users and business models, with clinicians reviewing outputs that affect patient care.


### Evidence-Based Clinician Q&A


The most direct product to build with Glass is a clinical question-and-answer tool for physicians, advanced practice providers, pharmacists, and nurses. A hospitalist asks whether a particular anticoagulant needs dose adjustment at a given renal function. A primary care physician asks what the current screening interval is for a patient with a specific risk profile. A pharmacist asks about a suspected interaction.


Glass supports evidence-based clinical Q&A grounded in current guidelines and literature, with citations that help clinicians examine the evidence behind an answer. A clinician can open the guideline behind a recommendation and judge its relevance to the patient. That makes the answer useful as a starting point for a decision, with its supporting evidence close at hand.


A team can build this as a standalone reference tool, a search experience inside a clinical application, or an assistant in a clinician portal. Glass provides the clinical reasoning and evidence grounding; the team shapes the experience around the questions its users need answered.


### Differential Diagnosis and Treatment Planning


Diagnostic reasoning is where a clinical specialist model separates itself most clearly from a general assistant. For differential diagnosis, Glass reasons across the history, exam, lab values, imaging, medications, and any other patient context your product supplies, and Glass is particularly strong at analyzing large amounts of unstructured patient data. Long free-text histories, pasted lab panels, and imaging reports are exactly the input Glass is designed to work through.


For treatment planning, Glass generally produces an assessment and plan that includes an overall analysis of the patient, problem-based assessments for the major active issues, diagnostic next steps, and treatment or management next steps. That structure mirrors how clinicians already think and write, which makes the output usable rather than merely interesting.


A team can build a case-review assistant for residents that takes a de-identified presentation and returns a ranked differential with reasoning, or an admission workup helper that drafts a problem-based plan for the admitting physician to edit. A telehealth company can offer a pre-visit synthesis that organizes intake data into a preliminary assessment the treating clinician reviews before the encounter. In each case, the clinician remains the decision maker. Glass contributes structured, cited reasoning that gives that clinician a strong starting point and a visible chain of evidence to accept, adjust, or reject.


### Clinical Copilots Inside Workflow Tools


Many healthcare software companies are not building a new destination for clinicians. They are adding intelligence to a product clinicians already use: a care management platform, a specialty practice system, a population health dashboard, a pharmacy workflow tool. A copilot embedded in that product needs to answer questions in context, summarize what matters, and draft the next artifact without asking users to leave their work.


Glass fits this pattern because one API supports the range of tasks a copilot needs. The same model that answers a guideline question can summarize a complex patient's history, suggest diagnostic next steps, and draft a note or letter. A product team can build a sidebar assistant that reads the context already on screen within their product and offers a cited synthesis, a suggested plan, or a draft document, all from one integration.


Breadth matters commercially. A team that starts with Q&A may next add summaries, documentation, and patient-facing materials. Glass supports those related clinical capabilities, giving a product team room to expand with one clinical technology partner. Each new experience can build on the same commitment to useful, evidence-based clinical work.


### Patient Education and Plain-Language Materials


Clinicians spend a surprising share of their time translating medical decisions into language patients can act on. Glass generates patient-facing documentation in plain language, including discharge instructions, care plan summaries, medication guides, condition education, and return precaution instructions.


A hospital can build a discharge workflow within its own application that drafts patient instructions from the clinician's plan, ready for nurse review and personalization. A digital health company can generate condition education tailored to a patient's diagnosis and reading level. A pharmacy platform can produce medication guides that explain why a drug was prescribed, how to take it, and what side effects should prompt a call. A chronic care program can turn a care plan into a summary the patient keeps on their phone.


Patient materials still have to be clinically sound. Return precautions after a procedure and instructions for a new medication need clinical context as well as clear language. Glass brings clinical reasoning to that writing task. A team can create materials for clinician review that help patients understand the plan and the questions to raise with their care team.


### Care Navigation and Evidence-Based Triage


Patient-facing and nurse-facing intake products need to know when a situation is routine and when it is urgent. Glass supports evidence-based triage by evaluating patient-reported symptoms, vital signs, and intake data against clinical criteria, identifying high-risk features, and returning structured triage output that can support intake systems, nurse triage tools, and escalation logic in patient-facing or provider-facing products.


A team can build a symptom intake flow for a telehealth service that gathers a patient's complaint and vitals, asks Glass to evaluate the presentation against clinical criteria, and routes the visit to the appropriate care level based on the structured result and the organization's own protocols. A nurse advice line can build a decision-support panel that highlights high-risk features in a caller's report so the nurse can prioritize and document. A health system can add a navigation layer that helps patients understand whether their concern fits primary care, urgent care, or emergency care, with clear escalation paths.


For a care navigation product, the value is a clinically informed next step: a concern surfaced for a nurse, a high-risk feature brought to a clinician’s attention, or clearer information about seeking care. Glass supports the clinical reasoning behind those experiences. The care organization determines its protocols and who reviews or acts on the guidance.


### Clinical Documentation and Ambient Scribing


Documentation burden is one of the most reliably felt problems in medicine, and one of the most common reasons buyers evaluate a healthcare AI API. Glass can produce many forms of clinical documentation, including H&P, HPI, clinic notes, progress notes, discharge summaries, prior authorization letters, handoff notes, and patient handouts.


For encounter capture, the Glass Scribing API transcribes clinical encounters from audio recordings and optionally generates structured clinical notes, including SOAP notes, H&Ps, and visit summaries, directly from the recording. A team can build an ambient scribe within a telehealth platform or a clinic application that records the visit with consent, produces a transcript, and drafts the note in the format the practice uses. The clinician reviews, edits, and signs.


Beyond the encounter itself, Glass supports the documents that surround it. A revenue cycle product can draft prior authorization letters that cite the clinical rationale for a requested therapy. An inpatient tool can generate handoff notes that summarize active problems and pending items for the oncoming team. A discharge workflow can produce the discharge summary and the patient handout from the same underlying plan.


Documentation is part of a larger clinical experience. A team can use Glass to support a note, a treatment plan, and the patient-facing explanation that follows. The opportunity is a connected product that helps clinicians move between those tasks while retaining review and approval of the clinical work.


### Patient-Context Summaries for Busy Care Teams


Care teams are drowning in information they do not have time to read. A patient arriving in the emergency department may have years of notes, dozens of medications, and a specialist history spread across documents. A care manager taking on a new panel needs to understand each patient quickly. Glass is particularly strong at analyzing large amounts of unstructured patient data, which makes patient-context summarization a natural product to build.


A team can build a pre-visit brief within their product that takes the patient context the application already holds, asks Glass for a concise clinical synthesis, and presents the clinician with the active problems, relevant medications, recent changes, and open questions. A care coordination platform can generate a panel overview that flags patients whose recent data suggests deterioration. A specialty referral tool can produce a summary of the referral question and the pertinent history so the specialist starts the visit informed.


The opportunity is to make a long patient history easier for a care team to use. A clinically focused brief can organize the relevant context around the reason for the encounter, giving the clinician a starting point for review. Glass’s ability to work with unstructured clinical information makes it a compelling foundation for that experience.


### Clinical Agents and Subagents in Larger Systems


An increasing number of healthcare products are built as multi-step systems in which several automated components each handle part of a workflow. A scheduling agent, a documentation agent, and a billing agent might all need a clinical opinion at some point in their process. Glass is a strong choice for the clinical reasoning component of such a system.


A team can build an intake assistant that helps organize a patient’s concern for clinical review, or a care management assistant that prepares an evidence-based synthesis for a care manager. Glass supplies clinical reasoning for these broader product experiences, helping the team serve users who need more than administrative automation.


Glass can provide the clinical expertise within a broader agent product, including cited answers, patient-context summaries and draft care plans. That lets a team build around the healthcare experience it wants to offer. Our guide to[clinical AI for agent products](https://glass.health/resources/clinical-ai-api-for-agents) explores more of those possibilities.


## Why Clinical Evaluation Should Drive Your Choice


Buyers often compare healthcare AI options by demo quality. A better test is how the model performs on clinical work, measured by people qualified to judge it. Glass is evaluated by clinicians and benchmarked on clinical use cases using a 900-question clinical accuracy benchmark suite covering medical knowledge and reasoning, diagnostic reasoning, clinical note generation, and hallucination detection. On that suite, Glass 5.5 outperforms the leading frontier foundation models. That is a statement about our own clinical benchmark, and it is exactly the kind of evidence a clinical product team should demand from any vendor.


Independent evaluation adds another view. The[Medical AI Superintelligence Test](https://www.arise-ai.org/mast/technical) from the ARISE AI Research Network evaluates clinical systems on reasoning, safety and diagnostic performance, and Glass models appear on its preview leaderboard. Our guide to[clinical AI API benchmarks](https://glass.health/resources/clinical-ai-api-benchmarks) explains what those results mean for a buyer considering Glass. The evaluated model and the available API offering should be distinguished when making that decision.


Clinical accuracy and the ability to inspect supporting evidence belong in the same buying decision. Glass combines clinical evaluation with cited answers, giving a product team both performance evidence to consider and a way for users to examine the clinical content in their product.


## HIPAA-Supported Deployment from Day One


Compliance is often the point where healthcare AI projects stall. Glass is end-to-end HIPAA compliant, and organizations using the Glass Developer API in HIPAA-regulated workflows may obtain a Business Associate Agreement with us for API use. The BAA is available as a click-through agreement in[Glass API settings](https://glass.health/settings/api) .


The BAA covers Glass's role in processing the clinical context your product sends; your finished product carries its own compliance obligations as the application patients and clinicians actually use. During development and evaluation, we recommend using synthetic or de-identified patient data, which lets your engineers iterate freely before any protected information enters the workflow.


For founders and product leaders, the practical effect is that the compliance conversation with a health system customer starts from a firm footing. You can state plainly that the clinical reasoning component operates under a BAA and is designed for regulated use. That gives prospective customers a concrete basis for discussing Glass’s role in the product. Our overview of a[HIPAA-compliant AI API](https://glass.health/resources/hipaa-compliant-ai-api) covers the buyer considerations in more detail.

## Commercial Fit for Teams at Different Stages


Glass is designed to work for an early-stage startup validating a clinical concept as well as for an established healthcare organization adding intelligence to an existing platform. Access to the Glass Developer API starts at a subscription minimum of $250 per month, with usage above that floor charged separately. For a founding team, that means a clinical model with evidence grounding, citations, and a BAA is available at a cost comparable to a few software seats, which lowers the barrier to building a credible prototype.


For larger organizations, the same API supports a program of related features from a single vendor relationship. A health system innovation group can pilot a documentation assistant, extend to patient education, and add a triage layer without re-running vendor selection each time. Product leaders at digital health companies can plan a roadmap knowing the clinical component will support the next feature as well as the current one.


The choice criteria are consistent across stages. If your product's value depends on clinical reasoning being correct, sourced, and reviewable, and if you would rather build your product than build a medical evidence pipeline, Glass is the fit. If your use case is administrative and never touches clinical judgment, a general model may serve you well, and we will not pretend otherwise.


## Frequently Asked Questions About Choosing Glass Health


### Why choose Glass Health instead of building on a general-purpose model?


Building clinical features involves evidence sourcing, clinical reasoning, citations and evaluation. Glass brings those capabilities together in a clinical API. Choosing Glass lets your team concentrate on the product experience while drawing on clinical capabilities already designed for healthcare work.


### Do Glass responses include citations?


Yes. Glass supports clinical answers with citations so users can examine the sources behind the information. That gives a clinician or care team a more useful basis for review and makes evidence part of the product experience.


### Which clinical use cases does Glass support?


Glass supports evidence-based clinical Q&A, differential diagnosis, treatment planning, documentation, patient education, triage, and patient-context summaries. The Glass Scribing API also supports encounter transcription and note generation. Together, these capabilities serve a broad range of clinical product ideas.


### Can Glass be used in HIPAA-regulated workflows?


Yes. Glass is end-to-end HIPAA compliant, and organizations using the Glass Developer API in regulated workflows may obtain a Business Associate Agreement through a click-through process in Glass API settings. Your finished product retains its own compliance responsibilities, and we recommend synthetic or de-identified data during development and evaluation.


### How is Glass evaluated for clinical performance?


Glass is evaluated by clinicians and benchmarked on a 900-question clinical accuracy suite covering medical knowledge and reasoning, diagnostic reasoning, clinical note generation, and hallucination detection. Glass 5.5 outperforms the leading frontier foundation models on that suite. Glass models also appear on the independent MAST preview leaderboard. We encourage every team to evaluate the API on its own intended use as well.


### Does Glass connect to my patients' records on its own?


No. Glass processes the clinical context your product supplies. Your application decides what information to send and what to do with the response, and Glass does not independently retrieve charts, send orders, or take clinical actions. This keeps control of data and workflow within your product and under your organization's policies.


### How quickly can a team start building with Glass?


A team can create an account, review and accept the BAA if needed, and begin building the same day from Glass API settings. Development can proceed with synthetic or de-identified data while you evaluate outputs for your use case, and the developer documentation is available as a supporting reference once you are ready to integrate.
